title: How plants and animals share one tree and its soil
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NCERT Class 3 'Plants and Animals Live Together': how plants and animals help each other, animals' habits and habitats, soil and the life in it, and bird sounds. No textbook needed.
summary: A tree at two in the afternoon can look empty. Visit it at dawn, at sunset and after dark, and it is full of animals. Your child studies one tree and the soil under it. They find out what soil is made of and who makes it. They map who uses each part of the tree, and how plants and animals help each other. They watch one animal's habits closely. Last, they find that some animals are awake by day and others by night, and each has its own call.
builds_on: Class 1: every place is somebody's home. Class 2: the word habitat, small habitats inside big ones, and how cactus, lotus, fish and camel suit their homes. Next, Class 4 visits India's deserts, mountains, plains and coasts. Class 5 studies adaptation, animals found in only one place, and predators and prey.
goals: By the end your child can say what soil is made of and why earthworms matter.
By the end your child can map at least eight living things in the layers of one tree and say what each gets from it.
By the end your child can give three ways animals help plants and three ways plants help animals.
By the end your child can watch one animal for ten minutes and record its habits.
By the end your child can explain that some animals in a habitat are awake by day and others by night, and that they eat different foods.
By the end your child can name two scientists who learned by watching and listening patiently.

the dark, crumbly part of soil made from rotted leaves and dead things
a living thing, like a worm, fungus or bacterium, that breaks dead things down into soil
what an animal usually does: when it eats, sleeps, rests and nests
the top layer of leaves and branches of a tree or forest
to carry pollen from one flower to another so seeds can form
a place where birds or bats rest or sleep
an animal's own way of living in a habitat: what it eats, where and when
all the sounds of a place together

earthworms and other decomposers make soil
seeds hide in soil, waiting (the seed bank)
a tree has layers of homes: roots, trunk, branches, canopy
animals use plants for food, shelter, nests and rest

days.title: Is this tree empty?
days.goal: Recall habitats and meet the idea that one place holds many lives, some of them hidden.

steps.title: Habitat recall
steps.do: Ask: 'What five things does a habitat give an animal?' Good answers: food, water, shelter, space and the right temperature. Ask: 'How does a cactus suit the desert? How does a lotus suit a pond?' Good answers: the cactus stores water in its thick stem, and the lotus has waxy leaves that float. Then say: 'This week we will study ONE place closely and find out how everyone in it lives together.'

steps.title: The two-minute look
steps.do: Choose a tree near your home: in the street, in the colony compound, or one you can see well from a window or balcony. Go there in the hot middle of the day if you can. Look at it for exactly two minutes. Then ask: 'How many animals did you see?' Write the number. At midday there are often very few. Ask: 'Does that mean nothing lives here?' Write your child's answer and keep it, because you will come back to it on Day 7.

steps.title: Story: The Night Tree
steps.do: Read the story 'The Night Tree' aloud, without explaining it. Then ask the story questions, especially: 'Why did the grown-ups think the tamarind tree was empty?' and 'How did Karthik know it wasn't?'

steps.title: Plan the tree diary
steps.do: Start the project. The tree you just looked at is your diary tree, so give it a name. Make a diary page with four rows: early morning, midday, sunset and after dark. Fill in the midday row now. Ask: 'Who do you think we will meet at each time?' Write the guesses. You will check them over the week.

days.title: What is soil made of?
days.goal: Find out what soil is made of, who makes it, and what is waiting inside it.

steps.title: Feel, smell, look
steps.do: Collect a handful of soil from each of three places: under a street tree, from a potted plant, and from a bare patch of ground. Spread each on newspaper. Your child feels each one (gritty, sticky or soft?), smells it, and looks with a magnifying glass for bits of leaf, root, stone and tiny animals. Ask: 'Which soil looks most alive? Why?' Then tell them the earthy smell of soil is made by bacteria, living things too small to see.

steps.title: Soil jar test
steps.do: Do Experiment e1 with the soil from under the tree. First ask: 'When we shake soil in water and let it stand, what do you think will happen?' Then shake it and leave the jar to settle until tomorrow.

steps.title: Seeds hiding in the soil
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Spread soil from under the tree in a tray, water it and put it in light. Add no seeds. Ask: 'Will anything grow if we plant nothing?' Write down the guess. This takes up to two weeks, so check it every few days.

steps.title: Charles Darwin's worms
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v1, the scientist Charles Darwin. He studied earthworms on and off for over 40 years. He measured how much soil they pushed up, and watched stones slowly sink as worms dug underneath them. He also tested whether worms can hear. His son played the bassoon, a loud wind instrument, next to pots of worms, and they did nothing. Then he put the pots on a piano and struck a note. The worms quickly went down into the soil. Ask: 'Why did the worms react to the piano but not the bassoon?' Good answer: they felt the shaking of the piano through the pot. Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Soil is…
steps.do: Your child finishes the sentence: 'Soil is made of…' Good answer: tiny bits of rock, humus from rotted leaves, air, water and living things. Then say: 'So soil is a habitat. Many things live in it.'

need: soil from three places (a street tree, a potted plant, a bare patch)
a tall clear jar with a lid

days.title: Who lives in the soil?
days.goal: Meet the soil animals and see how they turn dead things into new soil.

steps.title: Read the soil jar
steps.do: Look at the jar from Experiment e1. Your child draws the layers: small stones at the bottom, then sand, then fine silt, with cloudy clay settling on top and bits of leaf (humus) floating at the surface. Ask: 'Why did the stones sink first?' Good answer: bigger, heavier pieces sink faster through water.

steps.title: Soil animal count
steps.do: Under a street tree or a hedge, scrape up two handfuls of fallen leaves and the soil just below them onto newspaper. Spread it slowly with a spoon and look closely with the magnifying glass. Count and sort what you find. You may see earthworms, ants, beetles, woodlice, millipedes (many legs, slow, curl up when touched), centipedes (fast and flat, do not touch, they can bite), springtails (tiny jumping specks), white fungus threads and roots. For each one ask: 'Does it eat leaves, other animals, or both?' Finding only ants and fungus threads is normal, so try a second spot if you can. Put everything back where it came from, and wash hands afterwards.

steps.title: Where do leaves go?
steps.do: Find leaves at different stages: fresh and green, dry and brown, full of holes, and almost gone. Lay them in a line from fresh to almost soil. Ask: 'Who made the holes? Where does the leaf go?' Wait for guesses. Then explain: worms pull leaves underground and eat them. Woodlice and millipedes chew them. Fungi and bacteria finish the job. What is left is humus, which feeds new plants. Living things that break down dead things are called decomposers. Ask: 'If there were no decomposers, what would the ground under a tree look like after 100 years?'

steps.title: The circle
steps.do: Your child draws a circle with four arrows: the tree drops a leaf, a worm eats the leaf, the worm's droppings become soil, the soil feeds the tree. Ask: 'What would happen to the tree if there were no worms or other decomposers?' Then check the seed tray from Experiment e2, and water it lightly if it is dry.

need: leaves at different stages of rotting

days.title: The tree town
days.goal: Map who uses each layer of a tree for food, shelter, nests and rest.

steps.title: Tree layer survey
steps.do: Go to your diary tree in the early morning, before 8 am if you can. Look at four parts with Worksheet ws1, Section A: the roots and ground, the trunk and bark, the branches, and the canopy (the top leaves) with any flowers or fruit. Use your eyes and ears. For each living thing, write what it uses the tree for: food, shelter from sun and rain, a nest, or rest. Look for ant trails on the bark, a hole in the trunk, a squirrel's untidy nest of twigs, a crow's nest, caterpillars, spiders, and lichen (flat grey-green patches on the bark). Bird droppings under one branch show a roost, a place where birds sleep.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Back home, finish Worksheet ws1, Sections B and C. Read the questions aloud and let your child write or say answers. For the written 'why' questions, help them write one full sentence each.

steps.title: Diary: early morning
steps.do: Fill in the 'early morning' row of the tree diary. Compare it with the midday count from Day 1. Ask: 'Why were there more animals this morning?' Good answer: many birds feed in the cool early hours and rest in the heat of the day.

days.title: Plants need animals too
days.goal: See how plants depend on animals, and watch one animal's habits like a scientist.

steps.title: Flower watch
steps.do: Sit by a flowering plant for 8 minutes. Hibiscus, ixora, marigold, lantana, or a drumstick or mango tree in flower all work. A potted plant on a balcony gets fewer visitors, so use a plant outside if you can. Count every visitor: bees, butterflies, wasps, flies, sunbirds, ants. Look for yellow pollen on their bodies. Ask: 'What is the bee getting from the flower?' Then explain: while it drinks nectar, pollen sticks to it, and it carries the pollen to the next flower. This lets seeds form, and it is called pollination. Ask: 'So what does the bee give the flower?'

steps.title: Who plants the trees?
steps.do: Show a mango stone, a ber seed, a fig or a tamarind pod. Ask: 'How might this seed travel away from its parent tree?' Good answers: a bird or a bat eats the fruit and drops the seed far away, a monkey eats the fruit and throws away the stone, or a seed with hooks sticks to an animal's fur. Say: 'Peepal and banyan trees often grow out of walls and roofs. Birds ate their figs and dropped the seeds there.' Check Experiment e2: has anything sprouted? Count the seedlings.

steps.title: Animal habit watch
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Choose one animal you can watch for 10 minutes without disturbing it: a squirrel, a myna, a crow, a pigeon, a line of ants, or a street dog resting. Every minute, your child writes or draws what it is doing: eating, looking around, cleaning, resting, calling, chasing. Then ask: 'What did it do most? What did it seem to be watching for?'

steps.title: Jane Goodall watches
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v2, Jane Goodall. In 1960, with no university degree, she went to Tanzania in Africa to watch chimpanzees. For months they ran away from her. She kept coming back and sitting quietly. One day she saw a chimpanzee she called David Greybeard push a grass stem into a termite mound and pull it out covered in termites. He was using a tool. Ask the voice question. Then ask: 'What did your 10 minutes of watching show you that a quick look would not?'

need: a fruit with a seed (mango, ber, fig or tamarind)

days.title: Listening to a habitat
days.goal: Use sound to find out who lives in a place and see how they share it.

steps.title: Sound map at dusk
steps.do: Around sunset, go to your diary tree, or sit at a window or balcony. Your child puts an X in the middle of a sheet of paper. The X is them. They close their eyes for 5 minutes. Each time they hear a sound, they draw a small mark on the side it came from: a bird call, a cricket, a dog, a horn, leaves in the wind. Then open eyes and talk: which sounds were animals, and which were people or machines? Listen for parakeets and crows flying back to roost, mynas chattering, a koel, and bats. Fill in the 'sunset' row of the tree diary.

steps.title: Why do birds call?
steps.do: Explain that birds make two main kinds of sound. Calls are short. They mean things like 'danger!', 'I am here' or 'food here'. Songs are longer, and are often sung by males in the breeding season. A song says 'this is my place' and helps attract a mate. Many birds sing most at dawn, and this is called the dawn chorus. Copy four sounds together: the crow's 'kaa', the koel's rising 'ku-OO', the myna's chatter and the coppersmith barbet's 'tuk-tuk-tuk'. Ask: 'Why might a bird sing loudest at dawn?' Scientists have a few ideas. The air is often still at dawn, so sound travels far. It is also too dark to find food yet.

steps.title: The animal orchestra
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v3, Bernie Krause. He recorded the sounds of wild places for decades. He thinks that in a healthy habitat, animals call at different pitches and different times, like instruments in an orchestra, so each one can be heard. Play your sunset recording if you made one, or listen again tomorrow morning. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet and a family orchestra
steps.do: First make a family 'tree orchestra' for 3 minutes. Each person picks one animal sound from today: the crow's 'kaa', the koel's 'ku-OO', the barbet's 'tuk-tuk', a cricket's 'tsee-tsee' or an owlet's screech. First everyone calls at once. Then try again, taking turns, each with its own pitch. Ask: 'Which way could you hear each animal?' That is Krause's idea. Then do Worksheet ws2 together, reading each item aloud.

days.title: The night animals, and teach it back
days.goal: Meet the night animals, play the game and teach it all back.

steps.title: Night visit to the tree
steps.do: After dark, visit your diary tree with a grown-up. Cover a torch with red cellophane or a thin cloth, because a dim red light disturbs most animals less. First stand in the dark for 3 minutes and listen. Then shine the torch on the bark and leaves. Look for geckos, moths, spiders weaving webs, crickets, a frog, an owlet's eyes, and bats flying past. Fill in the 'after dark' row of the tree diary. Ask: 'Who was here at night that we never saw in the day?'

steps.title: Tree Town Shifts card game
steps.do: Play the card game g1. Players collect sets of four animals from the same part of the tree, and say whether each one is awake by day or by night.

steps.title: Dance: one day in the tree
steps.do: Play or hum soft music, and act out one whole day of the tree in four minutes. Dawn: flutter and sing like birds waking up. Midday: droop and rest in the shade, with only the ants marching in place. Sunset: flap noisily and come home to roost. Night: glide silently like an owl, zigzag fast like a bat, and rub your hands like a cricket. Ask: 'Which time of day did you like being in best?'

steps.title: What changes a habitat?
steps.do: Ask: 'What happens to the animals of our tree if the tree is cut down? If bright lights are put up all night? If the fallen leaves under it are swept up and burned?' Let your child reason. Good answers: the animals lose their homes, night animals get confused by the light, and the decomposers lose their food. Then ask: 'What could our family do to help the animals of our tree?'

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child shows the tree diary to the family and explains what soil is made of, how worms make soil, who lives in each part of the tree, how plants and animals help each other, and which animals are out by day and by night. Ask the check questions. Read out the Day 1 answer to 'Does that mean nothing lives here?' and ask if they still agree. For extra thinking, do Worksheet ws3.

need: a torch with red cellophane or cloth

worksheets.title: The tree town and the soil

sections.p: Write what you found in each part of the tree, and what it uses the tree for: food, shelter, a nest or rest.
Each of these animals is on or under a tree. What is it using the tree for?
The dark, crumbly part of soil made from rotted leaves is called ____.
You shook soil in a jar of water and let it settle. Which part settled at the very bottom?
How do earthworms help the soil?
opts: pulling leaves underground and mixing the soil, leaving air tunnels

sections.p: Match the soil animal to what it does.
pairs: eats dead leaves and makes soil
break down dead wood and leaves
carries food back to its nest

sections.p: You looked at your tree at midday and again in the early morning. Why did you see more animals in the early morning?
Give one way the tree helps animals and one way animals help the tree.
Is each animal mostly awake in the day or at night?
An animal that is awake at night is called ____.
What is the dawn chorus?
opts: birds singing a lot at sunrise

sections.p: A crow, a bee and a caterpillar all live on one mango tree. Why do they not fight over food?
opts: each eats a different food from a different part
the tree is too big to fight on

sections.p: Each animal has its own way of living on a tree, called its niche. Match each animal to its niche.
pairs: hunts insects and mice at night
digs insects out of the bark
eats fruit at night and drops the seeds

sections.p: In the breeding season, a male bird sings a long song from the same branch every morning. What is the song most likely saying?
A city puts bright lights around a park all night. Which animals might be affected, and how?
Peepal trees often grow out of walls. People think birds ate the figs and dropped the seeds there. How could you check this in your own street?
In Experiment e2 you put plain soil in a tray and planted nothing. Seedlings still grew. What does this show?
opts: soil holds hidden seeds waiting for the right conditions

sections.p: Decomposers are living things, like worms and fungi, that break down dead things. If they all disappeared, what would be the biggest problem?
opts: dead leaves and bodies piling up and plants running out of food from the soil

sections.p: The scientist Charles Darwin kept worms in pots. A loud bassoon played next to them made no difference. When he put a pot on a piano and struck a note, the worms went down into the soil. What does this show?
opts: worms hear sound through the air
worms feel shaking through what they touch

sections.p: Is each one an animal that helps plants, or a plant (or part of a plant) that helps animals?
cats: a plant (or part) that helps animals

sections.p: All the sounds of a place together are called its ____.
In the story 'The Night Tree', the grown-ups looked at the tree at two in the afternoon and said it was empty. What mistake did they make? How could a scientist make the same mistake?
Jane Goodall studied wild chimpanzees. She gave each chimpanzee a name, not a number. Some scientists said this was wrong. What do you think, and why?
Imagine you are an earthworm. Describe one day in your life, from what you eat to where you go.

experiments.title: Soil jar test: what is soil made of?
experiments.question: What different parts is soil made of?
need: a tall clear jar with a lid
soil from under a tree (enough to fill a third of the jar)
a pinch of salt (helps clay settle)
steps: Fill the jar one third with soil.
Add water until it is nearly full, and the pinch of salt.
Close the lid tightly and shake hard for one minute.
Put it down where it won't be moved. Look after 1 minute, 1 hour and the next morning.
Draw the layers and label them.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'When we stop shaking, will the soil all sink together or in layers? What will be at the bottom?'
experiments.observe: Small stones sink at once, and sand within a minute. Fine silt settles over an hour. Clay settles last, slowly, overnight or longer. Bits of leaf and twig (humus) float on top. The water may stay cloudy for a day or two.
experiments.why: Soil is a mixture of rock broken into pieces of different sizes, plus humus from dead plants and animals, plus air and water in the gaps. Bigger, heavier pieces sink through water fastest. Clay pieces are so tiny that they sink very slowly. Different soils have different amounts of each. Sandy soil lets water drain fast. Clay soil holds water and gets sticky. Soil with a lot of humus is dark and full of life.

experiments.title: Seeds hiding in the soil
experiments.question: Are there seeds hiding in ordinary soil?
need: a shallow tray or old plate with a few holes
soil from under a tree or a garden corner
steps: Spread the soil about 2 cm deep in the tray. Do NOT add any seeds.
Put it in a light place, like a windowsill, and keep it damp.
Check every 2–3 days for two weeks. Count the seedlings and draw them.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'If we plant nothing, will anything grow?'
experiments.observe: Usually a few kinds of seedlings appear within one or two weeks, often grasses and small weeds. If nothing grows, the soil may have come from a bag of bought potting mix, so try soil from under a street tree or an empty plot.
experiments.why: Soil holds a 'seed bank'. It has seeds dropped by plants, blown in by wind or left in bird droppings. Some lie still for years until they get water, warmth and light. When ground is cleared or dug, these hidden seeds sprout. This is one reason a forest can grow back after it is cut.

activities.title: Animal habit watch
steps: Choose one animal you can watch for 10 minutes without scaring it.
Make a table with ten rows, one for each minute.
Each minute, write or draw what it is doing: eating, resting, cleaning, looking around, calling, chasing, moving.
Count which behaviour came up most.
Write two sentences: what it does most, and what it seemed to be watching or listening for.
activities.outcome: A minute-by-minute record of one animal's habits, and two sentences about what it showed.

project.title: A day in the life of one tree
steps: Choose and name one tree on Day 1. Make a diary page with four times: early morning, midday, sunset, after dark.
Write your guesses of who you'll meet at each time.
Visit at each time this week. Write and draw every living thing you see or hear, and what it is doing.
Compare the four times: which was busiest? Who was only there at night?
Present the diary to the family on Day 7.
project.outcome: A four-time diary of one tree, showing its day shift and night shift.

game.title: Tree Town Shifts
rules: Cut out the 24 cards and shuffle them. Deal 5 cards to each player. Put the rest face down as the pile.
A set is 4 cards from the same group: ROOTS AND SOIL, TRUNK, BRANCHES, FLOWERS AND FRUIT, CANOPY or NIGHT SHIFT.
On your turn, ask any player for a card from a layer: 'Do you have someone from the TRUNK?' If they have one, they give it to you. If not, take a card from the pile.
When you collect a set of 4, lay it down. For each card, say whether the animal is awake by day or by night, and what it uses the tree for.
When the pile runs out, the player with the most sets wins.

cards.back: day and night: eats dead leaves
day and night: nests at the roots
day and night: breaks down dead wood
day and night: grows on the bark
day and night: its young eat wood under the bark
day: hunts insects on the trunk
day: sews leaves into a nest
day and night: webs between twigs
day: eats fruit, nests in holes

big: If a place looks empty, how can we be sure it is?
Does a tree belong to the people who own the land, or to everyone who lives in it?
Who works harder for the forest: the tiger or the earthworm?
If you could only use your ears, what would you know about the world that you don't know now?
Should animals be given names by scientists, or numbers?
Is a tree one living thing, or a home for many living things? Or both?

challenge.q: People often call soil 'dirt', as if it were dead and dirty. Is it?
challenge.hint: One teaspoon of healthy soil can hold more living things than there are people in India. Most are bacteria and fungi, too small to see. The earthy smell after rain comes partly from geosmin, a chemical made by soil bacteria. Is 'dirt' the right word?

challenge.q: How many kinds of living things can one tree be home to?
challenge.hint: One big tree may hold hundreds of kinds of insects, spiders, birds, lichens and fungi, plus many more in the soil beneath it. Scientists who counted the insects on single rainforest trees found many kinds that had never been named. How would you count everything living on your tree?

challenge.q: We often hear that earthworms cut in half become two worms. True?
challenge.hint: Mostly not. Sometimes the front part, with the head, can survive and regrow a tail, but the back part usually dies. Only some kinds of worms can regrow much. Why do you think this myth spread?

perspectives.view: I swallow soil and dead leaves every day. What comes out of me is richer soil. My tunnels let air and rain reach the roots. Ask: who matters more for growing your food, a farmer or a worm? Can you choose?

Many farmers leave old neem, mahua and banyan trees standing in their fields. The trees give shade, fodder for animals, fruit, and homes for birds that eat crop pests. Ask: what does a tree in a field give that a farmer cannot buy?
People who are blind often know a place by its sounds, smells and the feel of the air. Ask: what can be learned about a habitat by listening that cannot be learned by looking?

voices.idea: Darwin's last book, The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms (1881), showed that earthworms make and mix soil. He measured how much soil worms bring to the surface, and watched stones and old ruins slowly sink as worms dug beneath them. He also tested their senses. Worms ignored a bassoon and shouting, but went down into the soil when their pots were put on a piano and a note was struck.
voices.then: Many people thought worms were pests, or too small to matter. Some doubted Darwin's estimates of how much soil they moved. Still, the book sold very well.
voices.now: Darwin was right that earthworms are among the most important builders of soil in many places. Scientists still argue about the exact numbers, which vary from soil to soil.
voices.ask: Darwin was famous, but he chose to study something everyone ignored. What small living thing near you do you think deserves 40 years of study?

voices.idea: In 1960 Jane Goodall, a young woman with no university degree, began watching chimpanzees at Gombe in Tanzania. After months of patient sitting, she saw a chimpanzee she named David Greybeard strip leaves off a stem and use it to fish termites out of a mound. She showed that chimpanzees make and use tools, hunt, and have strong family bonds and their own personalities.
voices.then: Many scientists said only humans made tools. Some criticised her for naming the chimpanzees instead of numbering them, and for describing their feelings. Her mentor, Louis Leakey, said the finding meant people would have to rethink what makes humans special.
voices.now: Her findings are accepted. Many animals, including crows, elephants and octopuses, are now known to use tools. Studying animals as individuals with feelings is normal science.
voices.ask: Why do you think it took a person who sat quietly for months, rather than someone who visited for a day, to see the chimpanzees use tools?

voices.idea: Krause, a musician, spent decades recording the sounds of wild places around the world. He noticed that in healthy, undisturbed places the animals seemed to call at separate pitches and separate times, like instruments in an orchestra, so each could be heard. In the 1990s he called this the 'acoustic niche' idea. He named the sounds made by living things 'biophony'.
voices.then: Some ecologists liked the idea and began using sound recordings to check the health of forests and reefs. Others found places where many animals call at the same pitches and times, so the orchestra pattern is not always there.
voices.now: Listening to habitats, called soundscape ecology, is now a real tool for scientists. Whether animals truly share out the sound the way Krause suggested is still argued. It seems to happen in some places and not others.
voices.ask: If you recorded your street at dawn now and again in ten years, what might the difference tell you?

story.title: The Night Tree
text: Karthik had never seen the old tamarind tree in the corner of the colony park, but he knew it better than anyone.

He had been blind since he was born. He knew the park by its edges: the cool damp under the hand pump, the hot iron of the swing chain, the rough bark of the tamarind, cracked into deep ridges like the skin of an elephant's knee. He knew it by smell: in March, the sour-sweet of tamarind pods. After rain, the wet earth under its roots. And he knew it by its sounds.
That was why he sat very still on the bench when the uncles from the residents' committee came to stand under it, one hot Sunday afternoon.
"It's dead, practically," said Menon Uncle. "Look at it. No birds. Nothing. Just drops leaves all over the cars."
"And the roots are cracking the path," said someone else.
"Cut it," said Menon Uncle. "We'll get four more parking spots. We'll vote on it next Sunday."
Karthik's mother, beside him, said nothing, but he felt her hand go tight on his.

It was true that the tree was quiet. It was two o'clock, and the heat lay on the park like a blanket. Karthik listened hard. A car horn, far away. A fan in somebody's window. The dry tick of a leaf landing. That was all.
But Karthik had heard the tree at other times.
That night he asked his mother for her old phone, the one with the voice recorder. "I need to make a recording," he said. "Four recordings."

At half past five the next morning, before the milkman, he sat on the bench under the tamarind with the phone on his knee. The dark was cool and blue-smelling. And then, as if someone had switched it on, the tree woke up. First one bird, a loud sweet whistle that rose and fell, over and over: a magpie robin, his mother said later. Then a chattering, bossy noise, many voices at once: mynas. Then a sound like a tiny hammer on metal, tuk, tuk, tuk, tuk, so regular he could count it: the coppersmith barbet. A squirrel scolding. A koel, far up, calling higher and higher as if climbing stairs. The air was so full of voices that Karthik laughed out loud.

At two in the afternoon, he recorded again. The tree was silent, as the uncles had said. He sat there anyway. After a long time he heard, very close to his ear on the trunk, the faintest scratching. He put out a finger and felt a line of tiny moving bodies going up the bark. Ants. Hundreds of them. Going somewhere, coming back. Working.

At sunset he recorded a third time, and the tree went mad. The parakeets came back. They came back in shrieking green gangs from wherever they had spent the day, and they argued and squabbled and rearranged themselves in the branches until the whole tree seemed to shake. Crows came in with heavy flaps. Then, slowly, the shrieks became mutters, and the mutters became rustles.
And then it was the night shift.

Karthik loved the night shift best. At ten o'clock, with his mother beside him, he sat under the tree in the dark, which for him was no different from the day, except that the air was softer. Crickets started up in the roots, a thin silver ringing. A gecko went tik-tik-tik somewhere on the trunk. Something leathery whooshed past his face, big and soft and sudden, and his mother whispered, "Bat," and then two more went past, heading for the fig trees on the main road. And then, from a hole high in the trunk that he had touched once, years ago, standing on his father's shoulders, there came a sharp, squabbling, chattering screech, two voices at once, like an argument between two very small, very cross grandmothers.
"Owls," said his mother, amazed. "Little owls. Karthik, there are owls living in that hole."
"I know," said Karthik. "They live there every year."

On Sunday the committee met under the tree at two o'clock, because that was when Menon Uncle was free. It was hot and still and silent. Karthik stood up, and his voice shook, but he held up the phone.
"You came at the wrong time," he said. "Everybody's sleeping now. You have to listen at the other times."
He pressed play.

The magpie robin. The mynas. The tuk-tuk-tuk. Then a long silence, with the faint scratch of ants. Then the roaring green racket of the parakeets coming home. Then the crickets, and the gecko, and the soft rush of bats, and the two little owls screeching from their hole, right above the heads of the people standing there.
Nobody said anything for a while. Menon Uncle looked up into the branches, squinting, as if he could see the sounds.
"Play the owls again," he said.
story.epiphany: Some animals are busy by day and others by night. Many birds are busiest at dawn and dusk and rest in the midday heat. At night, owlets, bats, crickets and geckos take over, while ants work at all hours. One tree is home to many animals, each using it differently. The grown-ups called the tree empty because they looked at the wrong time, and only with their eyes. Karthik knows the tree by its sounds through a whole day, so he can show it is full. The turn is Karthik's line 'You came at the wrong time'. The story doesn't say what the committee decides.
ask: Why did the grown-ups think the tamarind tree was empty?
What did Karthik hear at dawn, at midday, at sunset and at night?
Why do you think the birds were quiet at two in the afternoon?
What did Karthik know about the tree that the grown-ups didn't?
What do you think the committee decided? Why did Menon Uncle want to hear the owls again?

ideas.idea: Day animals and night animals share one place.
ideas.more: Diurnal animals are awake by day and nocturnal animals by night, so they can share one tree without meeting. To know who lives somewhere, you must look and listen at different times.

ideas.idea: Soil is alive and is made by living things.
ideas.more: Worms, millipedes, fungi and bacteria turn dead leaves into humus. Humus feeds new plants, which drop new leaves, and the circle goes on.

ideas.idea: Plants and animals need each other.
ideas.more: Plants give animals food, shelter, nests and rest. Animals pollinate flowers, carry seeds far away and make soil. Many peepal and banyan trees in cities grew from seeds dropped by birds.

ideas.idea: Sharing works because everyone lives differently.
ideas.more: On one tree, the bee drinks nectar, the caterpillar eats leaves, the woodpecker digs bark and the owlet hunts at night. Each has its own niche, so they don't all compete for the same thing.

unknowns: Nobody knows how many kinds of tiny living things live in a handful of soil. Most soil bacteria and fungi have never been named.
Do animals in a healthy habitat really divide up the sound space like an orchestra? Scientists are still testing this idea.
How do bright lights at night change the lives of moths, bats, frogs and owls in our cities? Research is only beginning, and the full effects are not known.

books.title: A Log's Life
books.author: Wendy Pfeffer
books.why: A big tree falls and becomes a home and food for beetles, fungi and many small animals, until it turns to soil and feeds a new tree. It shows decomposers and shared homes.

books.title: Diary of a Worm
books.author: Doreen Cronin
books.why: A funny worm's-eye diary of life underground, with real worm facts tucked inside.

books.title: The Great Kapok Tree
books.author: Lynne Cherry
books.why: A man falls asleep while cutting a rainforest tree, and the animals who live in it whisper to him why it matters. Shows the layers and lives of one tree.

books.title: Me... Jane
books.author: Patrick McDonnell
books.why: Jane Goodall as a little girl, watching animals with her toy chimpanzee, dreaming of Africa.

books.title: The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms
books.author: Charles Darwin
books.age: adult (read the bits about the piano and the sinking stones aloud)
books.why: Darwin's last book, still readable and full of patient, funny experiments with worms.

check.a: Tiny bits of rock (sand, silt, clay), humus from rotted leaves and dead things, air, water and living things.

check.q: What do earthworms and other decomposers do?
check.a: They break down dead leaves and other dead things into humus, mix the soil and make tunnels for air and water, so plants can grow.

check.q: Name four ways animals use a tree.
check.a: Food (leaves, fruit, nectar, insects on it), shelter, nests, rest or roost.

check.q: Name two ways animals help plants.
check.a: Pollinating flowers (bees, butterflies, sunbirds) and carrying seeds far away (birds, bats, monkeys). Worms also make the soil that plants grow in.

check.q: What do diurnal and nocturnal mean? Give an example of each.
check.a: Diurnal: awake in the day (myna, squirrel, butterfly). Nocturnal: awake at night (owl, bat, moth, gecko).
Short calls warn of danger, keep in touch or say 'food here'. Longer songs, often at dawn, say 'this is my place' and help attract a mate.

check.q: Why can a crow, a bee and an owlet all live on one tree?
check.a: Each uses a different part, eats a different food or is busy at a different time: each has its own niche.
